blurb: Bearded Belgian toy dog with a domed head and an almost human expression
description: The Griffon Bruxellois, or Brussels Griffon, is a small, sturdy toy dog from Belgium with a short nose, domed head and rough or smooth coat; alert and devoted.
answer: The Griffon Bruxellois, or Brussels Griffon, is a toy dog from Brussels, Belgium, descended from small terrier-like stable dogs. It weighs about 3.5 to 6 kg, has a domed head, short nose and expressive face, and is described as alert, proud and very attached to its owner.

body: The breed descends from the Smousje, a rough-coated stable dog kept to kill rodents; the small dog in Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Marriage is thought to be an early form. In the 19th century Belgian coachmen crossed these stable griffons with imported toy breeds, including the Pug and King Charles Spaniel, producing the modern type and its red and black-and-tan colours. The related Griffon Belge and Petit Brabançon differ only in coat and colour.

The first Griffon was registered in the Belgian studbook in 1883, and Queen Marie Henriette helped make the breed internationally known. The two World Wars nearly wiped it out in Belgium, and it survived largely through breeders in the United Kingdom.

The Griffon is a small, sturdy dog standing about 23 to 28 cm tall, with a domed head, short nose and underbite. Its humanlike face is said to have inspired the Ewoks. Coats are either wiry/rough or smooth, in red, black and tan, or black and reddish.

The FCI describes the breed as well balanced, proud and alert, neither timid nor aggressive, and very attached to its owner. The AKC notes a low threshold for loneliness and a sensitive nature that responds poorly to harsh training. Griffons often bond with one person, are said to be good with children who do not tease them, and usually get along with other pets, though they may try to dominate much larger dogs.

The smooth coat needs little grooming, while the wiry coat needs weekly attention. Sources give little detail on exercise; as a toy breed, its needs are generally modest. Its large, prominent eyes are easily injured, so owners are advised to watch for eye problems.

One 2024 UK study found a life expectancy of 13.3 years. Griffons should be tested for congenital defects, the most serious being syringomyelia and Chiari-like malformation. Other conditions reported in the breed include cleft palate, eye lacerations, cataracts, lens luxation and glaucoma, and some births require a Caesarean section.

faq.q: How big does a Brussels Griffon get?
faq.a: It is a toy breed, standing about 23 to 28 cm and weighing roughly 3.5 to 6 kg.

faq.q: How long do Brussels Griffons live?
faq.a: One 2024 UK study found a life expectancy of 13.3 years, slightly above the average for purebred dogs.

faq.q: Are Brussels Griffons good with children?
faq.a: They are described as very good with children provided they are not teased, though they are not very patient and are sensitive to rough treatment.
